statements.text: Transparency I think is something that we all need to fight for, especially as this emerging technology is coming at us so quickly. [...] I want to see if regulatory sandboxes have been part of your conversations. [...] Do you see regulatory sandboxes having success in the EU and whether or not do you think they will be successful in the United States?
statements.context: House hearing on federal agency use of AI, where Representative Langworthy questions witnesses on EU-style regulatory sandboxes.

statements.text: are you concerned that as AI systems become more mature and complicated, that criminals will have greater opportunity to commit heinous crimes, like child exploitation?
statements.context: House committee hearing examining federal agency use of artificial intelligence.

statements.text: I also wanted to bring up an executive order issued by the last administration requiring Federal agencies to post for public view most of their AI use cases. This is intended to give the public a view into the Administration's current and planned use of AI systems. But many of these agency inventories are missing or they are incomplete, according to a Stanford University AI Institute whitepaper which was issued last December.
statements.context: Congressman Langworthy questions a witness during a House hearing on federal agencies' use of AI.

statements.text: The protections, you know, have to be built at the same time as, you know, all of the fruits of what AI can bring us. They have to be there. Our most vulnerable, I believe, are those most likely to be harmed by, you know, a lot of this AI technology.
statements.context: Rep. Nick Langworthy questions a DHS witness during a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on federal AI use.

statements.text: While AI has numerous benefits that I am sure will be discussed here today, it has serious implications on our youth, especially when it comes to generative images and child exploitation. [...] With that being said, Dr. Prabhakar, I would like to ask you whether or not you see the NIST AI framework being taken up by the Federal Government in the same way that NIST cybersecurity work is being used today, and what steps, if any, that your office is taking to implement the AI framework?
statements.context: Opening statement and question during a House Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation hearing on federal AI adoption.

statements.text: effective guardrails and training are in place to ensure that it is ethical, and it is responsible in its use.
statements.context: Opening remarks by Rep. Langworthy at a congressional hearing on AI workforce readiness.

statements.text: It is chilling. [...] So, I wanted to ask you, what are the biggest gaps in the current legal framework that need to be filled?
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on deepfake harms, with Representative Langworthy questioning a witness about legislative and prosecutorial gaps.

statements.text: Thank you, Chairwoman Mace. It seems now every single week that goes by, we see another story about a bad actor using AI unethically. [...] that would create a commission examining generative AI safeguards, assess current statutes, and recommend legislative revisions to enhance law enforcement's ability to prosecute AI-related child exploitation crimes.
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing on deepfake-related harms, March 12, 2024.

statements.text: Mr. Shehan, how is law enforcement reacting to the uptick in AI-generated child sexual abuse material, CSAM? Has that approach been reactive as in waiting for images to circulate, or are there ways law enforcement can be more proactive?
statements.context: House committee hearing on deepfakes, with a member questioning a witness on law enforcement responses to AI-generated CSAM.

statements.text: This bill creates a commission that looks at the intersection of artificial intelligence and child sexual abuse material, specifically to support law enforcement and the ability to prosecute relevant cases.
statements.context: House Constitutional Authority and Single Subject statement for H.R. 8005 filed by Rep. Nick Langworthy.

statements.text: AI is no longer a theory about the future. It is already transforming the way we deliver care and how we diagnosis disease and how we use data to improve outcomes.
statements.context: Opening statement and question at a subcommittee hearing examining AI technologies in American healthcare, addressed to a witness identified as Mr. Toy.

statements.text: AI is not a replacement for doctors, nurses, or caregivers, but a tool to help them deliver beter care for more people.
statements.context: Closing remarks at a congressional hearing on AI in American health care.
